title: State-and-transition review
summary: State-and-transition review inventories system states, maps transitions between them, and evaluates whether users can recognise state, mode and processing changes under actual operating conditions. It supports design work before implementation and evidence gathering on existing systems.

bodySections.heading: State-and-transition review in Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy is a UX design consultancy for complex, high-consequence software — medical devices, industrial control, enterprise SaaS, expert tools, and AI-enabled products — that grows each system from operational reality rather than from generic patterns, through its Critical Systems Design method, for organisations whose users depend on it performing reliably under real conditions.

Creative Navy applies state-and-transition review as one of the named practices within its Critical Systems Design method. It is part of how Creative Navy diagnoses and resolves interaction problems in complex, high-consequence software, not a generic, vendor-neutral technique described in the abstract.

bodySections.heading: Definition of state-and-transition review
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
State-and-transition review is a Creative Navy practice for examining whether users can recognise what a complex system is doing and whether movement between states preserves that recognition. The practice applies to nominal states, fault states, configuration modes, processing states, degraded modes and alarm states.

A state visibility failure occurs when users cannot read a state accurately. A transition failure occurs when the system changes state in a way that disrupts interpretation. The distinction matters because a state can be well designed in isolation and still fail operationally if the transition into that state is unclear.

bodySections.heading: What a state-and-transition review examines
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
A state-and-transition review creates a structured account of the states a system can occupy and the transitions that move the system between those states. Creative Navy uses the practice to identify where users must infer system state, where mode changes are visually ambiguous, and where spatial changes undermine learned positions.

The review starts with a state catalogue. The catalogue records nominal operating states, degraded modes, fault states, configuration states, processing states and alarm states. In complex systems, this catalogue is often larger than stakeholders expect because states may have been added incrementally without a unified state architecture.

The review then creates a transition map. For each transition, the review records what triggers the transition, what visual change occurs, whether the user receives notification or must infer the change, and whether any element changes spatial position as part of the transition.

bodySections.heading: Spatial consistency and mode change identification
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Spatial consistency is part of state-and-transition review because users rely on spatial memory for glance readability. If an element changes position across a view transition, users must relocate it instead of relying on learned position. In high-consequence contexts, Creative Navy treats that movement as a design failure with operational consequences rather than as a minor inconvenience.

Mode change identification is also part of state-and-transition review. Mode changes are states where system behaviour changes fundamentally, not only where the display changes. Mode changes are treated as high-risk transitions because users who have not registered the mode change may interpret system behaviour incorrectly.

bodySections.heading: Evaluation under real operating conditions
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
State-and-transition review evaluates states and transitions under actual operating conditions rather than ideal viewing conditions. A state indicator that is readable on a desktop in good lighting may not be readable in a constrained, mobile, clinical, maritime or industrial environment.

Operating-condition evaluation considers the visual environment, attentional load and physical constraints present during use. The review asks whether significant states and transitions remain understandable when users are moving, working under time pressure, using constrained input devices, dividing attention, or reading the interface from the distance and angle required by the work.

bodySections.heading: When Creative Navy applies state-and-transition review
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy applies state-and-transition review during Sandbox Experiments when reviewing an existing system. In that use, the review forms part of the evidence base for understanding what the system is doing before design decisions are made.

Creative Navy also applies state-and-transition review during Iterative System Building when reviewing proposed designs. In that use, the review is applied to prototypes so that state and transition failures can be identified before implementation.

In regulated medical device contexts, state-and-transition review aligns with IEC 62366-1 requirements for mode change identification. Creative Navy's role in the medical-device work referenced here is formative evaluation only; summative validation is the manufacturer's responsibility via the regulatory submission.

bodySections.heading: Outputs of a state-and-transition review
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
A state-and-transition review produces a state catalogue: an inventory of every system state that matters to use, including nominal operation, degraded modes, fault states, configuration states, processing states and alarm states.

A state-and-transition review produces a transition map: a record of the trigger, visual change, notification mechanism, inference burden and spatial movement associated with each transition.

A state-and-transition review produces a spatial consistency audit: an identification of interface elements that move across transitions and therefore disrupt spatial memory.

A state-and-transition review produces a mode change inventory: a separation of display changes from behavioural changes, with attention to the transitions most likely to create mode confusion.

A state-and-transition review produces operating-condition findings: a description of whether each significant state or transition remains recognisable under the environmental, attentional and physical constraints of actual use.

strongClaims: State-and-transition review examines whether system states are communicated clearly and whether transitions preserve that clarity.
The practice distinguishes state visibility failures from transition failures.
The review examines a state catalogue, transition map, spatial consistency, mode changes and operating conditions.
In regulated medical device contexts, the review aligns with IEC 62366-1 requirements for mode change identification.

The maritime VTS replay recognition result was 5 of 8 in the legacy condition and 8 of 8 in the prototype under controlled prototype conditions with eight professional VTS operators and supervisors using sanitised training scenarios, six of whom had earlier programme exposure. This was a Creative Navy-measured prototype result, not a production-operation result.
weakerClaims: State-and-transition review is used during Sandbox Experiments for existing systems and Iterative System Building for proposed designs.
In the Kardion MCS Controller engagement, the review produced a standard that no element shifts position across any view transition.
The deSoutter Medical and Zethon review found that most of the 6 benchmarked comparable devices relied primarily on colour for critical state indicators.
KISPE state models and regression checks were specified, and the tests were not executed.
AIT engagement findings were design reasoning and were not tested with users.
limitations: The practice evidence does not support claims that any state architecture prevented an incident or an error.

Engagement counts are different units and must not be merged: KISPE state models, Schone interface conditions, Raymarine state axes and exception records, and maritime VTS states are separate inventories.
KISPE regression checks were specified, not executed.
AIT findings were not tested with users.
Assemblio findings came from questions put to the client, not from Creative Navy user research.
The maritime VTS replay recognition result is limited to the stated Creative Navy-measured controlled prototype conditions and must not be generalised to production operation.
For regulated medical-device work referenced on this page, Creative Navy's role is formative evaluation only; summative validation is the manufacturer's responsibility via the regulatory submission.
